sections.heading: Lead-Free Piezoelectric MEMS Energy Harvesters of $( \mathsf { K } , \mathsf { N a } ) \mathsf { N b } 0 _ { 3 }$ Thin Films on Stainless Steel Cantilevers
sections.text:
Yuichi Tsujiura1, Eisaku Suwa1, Fumiya Kurokawa1, Hirotaka Hida1, Kazufumi Suenaga2, Kenji Shibata2, and Isaku Kanno1

1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Kobe University, Kobe 657-8501, Japan   
2Hitachi Cable, Ltd., Tsuchiura, Ibaraki 300-0026, Japan

Received May 31, 2013; accepted June 25, 2013; published online September 20, 2013

We fabricated piezoelectric MEMS energy harvesters (EHs) of lead-free $( \mathsf { K } , \mathsf { N a } ) \mathsf { N b } { \mathsf { O } } _ { 3 }$ (KNN) thin films on microfabricated stainless steel cantilevers. The use of metal substrates makes it possible to fabricate thin cantilevers owing to a large fracture toughness compared with Si substrates. KNN films were directly deposited onto Pt-coated stainless steel cantilevers by rf-magnetron sputtering, thereby simplifying the fabrication process of the EHs. From XRD measurement, we confirmed that the KNN films on Pt-coated stainless steel cantilevers had a perovskite structure with a preferential (001) orientation. The transverse piezoelectric coefficient $\scriptstyle \theta _ { 3 1 , \mathrm { f } }$ and relative dielectric constant $\varepsilon _ { \Gamma }$ were measured to be $- 3 . 8 \mathsf { C } / \mathsf { m } ^ { 2 }$ and 409, respectively. From the evaluation of the power generation performance of a KNN thin-film EH (length: $7 . 5 \mathsf { m m }$ , width: $5 . 0 \mathsf { m m }$ , weight of tip mass: $2 5 \mathsf { m g } )$ ), we obtained a large average output power of $1 . 6 \mu \mathsf { W }$ under vibration at $3 9 3 \mathsf { H z }$ and $1 0 \mathsf { m } / \mathsf { s } ^ { 2 }$ . $©$ 2013 The Japan Society of Applied Physics

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Piezoelectric thin films have attracted attention for various micro sensors and actuators in micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) applications.1–4) $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { Z r } , \mathrm { T i } ) { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ (PZT) thin films have been mainly used in piezoelectric MEMS devices because of their excellent piezoelectric properties. Considering the toxic lead contained in PZT, however, lead-free piezoelectric materials with high piezoelectric properties are strongly required. As an alternative material for PZT, leadfree ones, such as $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ (BT), $( \mathrm { B i } , \mathrm { N a } ) \mathrm { T i O } _ { 3 }$ (BNT), and $( \mathrm { K } , \mathrm { N a } ) \mathrm { N b } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ (KNN), have been studied.5–8) Among these, KNN is expected as a promising candidate because of its high piezoelectricity and Curie temperature.9,10) Furthermore, it was reported that the KNN thin films on $\mathrm { P t / T i } /$ $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { S i }$ substrates showed a large transverse piezoelectric coefficient $e _ { 3 1 } ^ { * }$ of $- 1 4 . 4 \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ , which is comparable to that of PZT thin films.11)

In recent years, there have been many studies on energy harvesters (EHs) made of piezoelectric thin films functioning as power sources for small electronic devices, such as autonomous wireless sensor nodes.12–16) EHs are expected to replace batteries as maintenance-free power sources. In the case of piezoelectric MEMS EHs, they usually have unimorph cantilever structures constructed from piezoelectric thin films on Si substrates. Under vibrations with the resonant frequency of the cantilevers, the maximum output power can be obtained. However, the brittleness of KNN/Si unimorph cantilevers is a serious issue for practical application; overcoming this problem also enables not only to generate a large output power under resonant vibrations but also to reduce the resonant frequency of conventional MEMS EHs to that under environmental vibrations $( < 2 0 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ .17)

In this study, we fabricated piezoelectric MEMS EHs by depositing lead-free KNN thin films on metal cantilevers. The fracture toughness $K _ { \mathrm { I c } }$ of Si is less than $1 \mathrm { M P a } \mathrm { m } ^ { 1 / 2 }$ whereas that of austenitic stainless steel (SS304) is more than $1 0 0 \mathrm { M P a } \mathrm { m } ^ { 1 / 2 }$ .18,19) The large fracture toughness of metal cantilevers prevents the breakdown or cracking of the cantilevers and ensures the long lifetime of EHs.

We deposited KNN thin films directly onto the microfabricated stainless steel cantilevers by rf-magnetron sputtering. Subsequently, we measured the frequency response, load resistance dependence, and acceleration dependence of a KNN thin-film EH to evaluate power generation performance.

sections.heading: 2. Device Fabrication
sections.text:
KNN thin films were deposited on $\mathrm { P t }$ -coated ferritic stainless steel (SS430) cantilevers by rf-magnetron sputtering. By the direct deposition of the piezoelectric thin films on the microfabricated SS430 cantilevers, we eliminated the etching processes of the KNN films after the thin-film depositions and achieved the simple and low-cost fabrication process of EHs. The coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) of the KNN films and SS430 are about $8 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 }$ and $1 1 . 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } \mathrm { K } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively.10,20) Considering that the CTE of typical austenitic stainless steel (SS304) is $1 8 . 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } \mathrm { K ^ { - 1 } }$ , the small difference in CTE between the KNN films and SS430 can mitigate the initial bending of the unimorph cantilevers.

The fabrication process of EHs is schematically shown in Fig. 1. First, by the two-step spray etching of ferric chloride solution to $3 0 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick SS430 substrates with photoresist coatings on both sides, $3 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick cantilevers with tip masses were fabricated. This etching process enables us to fabricate the fixed end and the tip mass of cantilevers without bonding or clamping. These cantilevers were designed to have small sizes $( < 7 . 5 \times 5 . 0 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } )$ and low resonant frequencies $( < 4 0 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ .

Prior to KNN thin film deposition, a $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ oxide layer was deposited by plasma chemical vapor deposition (CVD) onto the microfabricated SS430 cantilevers to improve the adhesion of the KNN films to SS430. Then, $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ bottom electrodes were deposited on the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ oxide layer at the substrate temperature of $2 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ by rf-magnetron sputtering. Successively, the KNN films with a composition of ${ \mathrm { K } } / { \mathrm { N a } } =$ 45/55 were deposited on $\mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { T i } / \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { S S } 4 3 0$ cantilevers by rf-magnetron sputtering.9–11,21) During the deposition of the KNN films, the substrate was heated to around $6 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and deposition was performed under $\mathbf { A r } / \mathbf { O } _ { 2 }$ mixed gas atmosphere. The thickness of the KNN films was $2 . 2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . Subsequently, the Pt top electrodes were prepared through a shadow mask. sections.heading: 3. Piezoelectric Properties of KNN Films
sections.text:
We evaluated the crystal structure of the KNN films by X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurement. Figure 3 shows XRD patterns of the KNN films on the SS430 cantilevers. The diffraction of the perovskite KNN with a preferential (001) orientation was clearly observed, indicating that pyrochlorefree KNN films were prepared on the $\mathrm { P t }$ -coated SS430 cantilevers. We then measured the dielectric properties of the KNN films using an LCR meter (NF ZM2353). The relative dielectric constant $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } }$ of the KNN films on SS430 was as low as 409, which is lower than that of the KNN films on Si substrates $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } } \sim 8 0 0 )$ .22) The low relative dielectric constant of the KNN films is attributed to the in-plane compressive stress produced by the difference in CTE between the KNN films and the SS430 substrates. By contrast, the dielectric loss tan $\delta$ of the KNN films was as high as 0.56. A large dielectric loss might be related to the leakage current of the KNN films, which is attributed to the structure and residual stress of the KNN films.11)

The transverse piezoelectric properties of the KNN films were assessed by considering the inverse piezoelectric effect for the unimorph cantilevers.22,23) We applied a unipolar sinusoidal electric voltage across the top and bottom electrodes at a frequency sufficiently lower than the resonant frequency of the cantilever, and measured cantilever displacements using a laser Doppler vibrometer (Ono Sokki

sections.heading: 4. Power Generation Performance
sections.text:
Figure 5 shows a schematic diagram of the measurement setup for vibration EHs. The EHs were mounted on the vibration exciter (EMIC 512-A) and the acceleration pickup (EMIC 731-B) was attached to the base of the cantilevers for monitoring the acceleration amplitude. The top and bottom electrodes of the KNN films were connected to a load resistance and the generated voltage was measured using a frequency response analyzer (FRA; NF FRA5095). We evaluated the power generation performance (frequency response, load resistance dependence, and acceleration dependence) of the KNN thin-film EHs based on SS430 cantilevers. where $f _ { 0 }$ is the resonant frequency and $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are the frequencies of half-power points. From Eq. (3), the BW at $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ was calculated to be $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ , which is one and a half times larger than that at $1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . These results indicate that the nonlinear resonance causes a wider BW for the EHs. The softening effects are attributed to the round edge shape of the fixed end of the cantilever structure. Figure 7 shows the output power and output voltage as functions of the load resistance at the resonant frequency of $3 9 3 \mathrm { H z }$ at the acceleration amplitude of $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . The average output power $( P = V ^ { 2 } / 2 R )$ reached $1 . 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the optimum load resistance of $5 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . To evaluate the power generation performance, we defined the power density as the maximum output power divided by the volume of the cantilever, and it was calculated to be $0 . 4 1 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . On the other hand, we previously fabricated PZT EHs of the stainless steel cantilevers with the same configuration and evaluated the power generation performance.26) The KNN and PZT EHs are compared in Table I. From the evaluation of the power generation performance of the cantilever with the same design, the maximum output power of the PZT films was $6 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ (power density: $1 . 7 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )$ under the conditions of $3 6 7 \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, we presented the simple fabrication of piezoelectric MEMS EHs of lead-free KNN thin films on stainless steel (SS430) cantilevers. The stainless steel cantilevers with a built-in tip mass were produced by twostep spray etching. After the deposition of $\mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { T i } / \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ bottom layers on SS430, the KNN films were directly deposited on the cantilevers by rf-magnetron sputtering. The KNN films have a perovskite structure with a preferential (001) orientation. From the measurement of the dielectric and piezoelectric properties of the KNN films, a low relative dielectric constant $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { r } } ; 4 0 9 )$ with a high dielectric loss (tan -: 0.56) and a relatively high transverse piezoelectric coefficient $( e _ { 3 1 , \mathrm { f } }$ : $- 3 . 8 { \bf C } / { \bf m } ^ { 2 }$ ) were observed. From the evaluation of the power generation performance of the KNN EH (length: $7 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ , width: $5 . 0 \mathrm { m m }$ , weight of tip mass: $2 5 \mathrm { m g }$ ), a clear nonlinear resonance due to spring softening was observed at the resonant frequency of $3 9 3 \mathrm { H z }$ . The maximum output power and power density were 1.6 and $0 . 4 1 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ under the conditions of $3 9 3 \mathrm { H z }$ , $5 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and $1 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . These EHs exhibited high efficiency and robustness under environmental vibrations.
